text: I've been sitting with something all week and I want to write it out properly. When I left the firm three years ago I told everyone it was for my health, and it was, partly. But I think the truer reason was that I didn't like who I was becoming there: sharper, colder, always measuring people by how useful they were to me. Tonight at dinner Laila asked why I never talk about that job, and I didn't have a neat answer. I'm not ashamed of it exactly. I learned a lot. I just notice that I still flinch when someone praises me for being efficient, as if it's a compliment for the wrong thing. I want my next chapter to be built around something else. I'm not sure what yet. Curiosity, maybe. Kindness, definitely.

Today was the kind of day where everything lands on you at once. At eight the school rang because Noor had a temperature, so I left the office and collected her, then sat on the floor of her bedroom answering emails while she slept. At eleven the builder called to say the kitchen will be another three weeks because a part is on back order, which means another three weeks of washing dishes in the bath. At two my manager moved the client deadline forward to Thursday. At four Mum phoned in tears about her test results, which turned out to be fine, but it took an hour to get her calm. Now it's ten at night, the inbox has sixty unread messages, the washing machine is beeping and I genuinely do not know which of these things to do first. I'm just sitting here.

Second Christmas in this city and I spent it mostly on my own again. I had the invitation from Hiroshi's family but I said I was busy, because I couldn't face being the extra person at someone else's table, smiling through jokes I don't understand. So I cooked a small meal, watched the old films my dad used to love, and called home at the hour when everyone there was already half asleep. My sister passed the phone around and I heard the noise of the house, the dog, my nephew shouting about a present. When I hung up the silence in the flat was so complete I could hear the fridge. I keep telling myself next year will be different, that I'll have made more friends by then. I said that last year too. I'm tired of being the person who doesn't belong anywhere.

I had the first session with the new physio today and for the first time in two years someone actually explained what is going on in my back instead of just handing me a leaflet. She drew it on a whiteboard, showed me which muscles have basically gone to sleep and which ones have been doing all the work to compensate. Then she gave me four exercises, really boring ones, and said if I do them every day for six weeks I should notice a difference. I've heard promises before, so I'm not getting carried away, but there was something about how sure she was that has stayed with me all evening. I did the exercises again before bed. They hurt a bit. I'm going to do them tomorrow too. It feels like there might be a way back to running after all.

I'm writing this with my hands still shaking. The letter from the housing association arrived this morning: they are 'reviewing' our tenancy because of a complaint about noise, and the noise in question is my son, who is autistic and sometimes cannot help shouting when he is overwhelmed. They know this. It's in the file. I have sent them the doctor's letters twice. Nobody from the office has ever met him. Nobody has asked how we manage, or whether we need any support. They just send threatening letters with words like 'breach' and 'eviction' in bold. I spent an hour on the phone being transferred between departments until a woman told me to 'put it in writing'. I have put it in writing. I have put it in writing for three years. I am done being polite to people who treat my child as a nuisance.

Sunday, and I spent the whole of it doing almost nothing, which is exactly what I needed. Slept until nine, made a proper breakfast with eggs and the good bread, then sat in the garden with the paper while Marcus fiddled with the lawnmower and swore at it gently. In the afternoon we walked up the hill behind the village and back, slowly, stopping to look at the sheep and the view of the reservoir. Nothing special happened and nobody needed anything from me. I didn't check my work email once. Dinner was leftovers. Now the light is fading, the cat is asleep on my feet and there's a film on that neither of us is really watching. I feel full up in a quiet way, like everything is where it should be. I'd like more Sundays like this one.

We got the keys today. After eighteen months of saving, two offers that fell through, one surveyor who found a crack in a wall that turned out to be nothing, and a mortgage advisor who disappeared for a fortnight, we finally have a front door that is ours. Dani cried in the estate agent's office. I pretended not to and then cried in the car. We drove straight there and walked from room to room in the empty house saying things like 'this will be the reading corner' and 'the cot can go there'. The heating doesn't work and the kitchen is from about 1987 and I could not care less. We ate chips sitting on the floor of the living room. Moving day is Saturday and I want it to be Saturday right now. I can't stop smiling.

I want to write down how grateful I am to the people at the hospice, because I don't think I said it properly at the time. For the last three weeks of Dad's life they looked after him, and after us, as if we were the only family there. The nurse called Precious learned that he liked the radio tuned to the cricket and made sure it was on every morning. The volunteer, an old man called Stan, sat with Mum in the garden and talked about his own wife. When Dad died in the night, they let us sit with him as long as we wanted and brought us tea without asking. Nobody rushed us. Nobody made us feel like a bed was needed. I am going to write to them, and I am going to give them money every year for the rest of my life.

I sat by the canal for an hour after work today and let my mind go blank in a way that hasn't happened in months. The water was flat and green, a heron was standing on the far bank so still I thought it was a sculpture until it moved, and every so often a narrowboat chugged past with someone waving from the back. I watched the light change on the brick of the old warehouses. I didn't think about the project or the mortgage or the argument with my brother. I just sat. When I got up my legs were stiff and the air had gone cool and I realised I hadn't looked at my phone once. I walked home slowly. I want to remember that this is available to me, ten minutes from my front door, whenever I need it.

I gave my first full lecture today, an hour long, to a hall of about a hundred and twenty first-year students, and I didn't fall apart. I'd rehearsed it so many times that Amira can probably recite it, and I was still convinced I'd freeze or my slides would break or someone would ask a question I couldn't answer. In the end the projector worked, I made a joke that actually landed, and three students stayed behind to ask about the reading. One of them said it was the first lecture this term she'd actually understood. Walking back across the campus I felt about ten feet tall. Two years ago I couldn't speak in a seminar of eight people without my voice shaking. I know it's only one lecture and there are twenty more to go, but I did it, and I did it well.

The baby is three weeks old and I don't think I've slept more than two hours in a row since she was born. Jamal does the night feed when he can, but he's back at work, so most nights it's me pacing the landing with her on my shoulder at three in the morning, humming the same song over and over. During the day I do the washing in between feeds and forget to eat until the afternoon. My mother visits and tells me to sleep when the baby sleeps, which is lovely advice from someone who has not met this baby. I love her completely and fiercely and I am so tired that I put the milk in the cupboard and the cereal in the fridge this morning and didn't notice until lunch. My eyes ache. My bones ache. I'm going to try to sleep now.

I can't stop going over the conversation with the consultant. She was kind and very clear, but the words were 'further investigation' and 'we'd like to rule some things out', and my brain has filled in every gap with the worst possible version. The scan is on Friday, then the results take ten days. Ten days. I looked things up, which I know I shouldn't have done, and now I can't unsee the statistics. Tom keeps saying it's probably nothing and squeezing my hand, and I keep nodding, and then I go into the bathroom and stare at myself in the mirror trying to work out if I look ill. I've cleaned the kitchen twice tonight. I keep picking up my phone to text someone and putting it down again because I don't want to say it out loud.

A normal Tuesday, written down for the record. Up at 6:30, coffee, emails until eight. Dropped the kids at school, then a team meeting about the quarterly budget that ran over by twenty minutes. Spent the late morning reviewing contracts with Ines and the afternoon on a call with the Lisbon office about the supplier change. Picked up the dry cleaning on the way home and the ingredients for a stir-fry. Homework with the kids after dinner: fractions and a spelling list. Watched the news, loaded the dishwasher, put a wash on. Paid the electricity bill and booked the car in for its service next Thursday. Read a chapter of my book in bed. Nothing good or bad really happened. Just a day, the kind I'll have forgotten by next week, so here it is in writing.

I think I've been depressed for a while and only now have the words for it. Looking back over these pages, the last two months are full of entries that say 'tired', 'flat', 'couldn't be bothered', and I just thought it was the winter. I stopped going to choir. I stopped calling Bea back. I've eaten toast for dinner most nights. Today I couldn't make myself get out of bed until eleven, and when I did I sat on the edge of it for twenty minutes. I'm not in danger, I want to be clear about that, I'm just grey all the way through. I've booked a GP appointment for Thursday, which took everything I had. Writing this down is the first honest thing I've done in weeks. I want to feel like myself again. I'm not sure I remember how.

The meeting with the planning department was supposed to be thirty minutes and it took the whole afternoon. They lost the drawings we sent in March, then found them, then said they were the wrong version, then said the version they wanted had been superseded by a new form that nobody had told us about. Every person we spoke to was polite and none of them could make a decision. At one point I was asked to explain the extension three separate times to three different officers, each of whom took notes and none of whom seemed to read the previous person's notes. We left with a list of six new documents to provide and a promise that someone 'will be in touch'. It's been nine months. I just want to build a small kitchen for my family. Why is this so hard.

Long day at the allotment and I'm writing this with soil still under my fingernails. The broad beans are finally up, the onions look strong, and the rhubarb that Mr. Patel gave me as a cutting two years ago has gone completely wild. We shared a flask of tea on the bench between our plots and he told me about the garden his father kept in Gujarat, mangoes and chillies and a well he used to drop stones into as a boy. I told him about my grandmother's roses. Neither of us said much after that, we just sat and looked at our rows. On the walk home I felt properly content, the kind of tired that comes from using your body for something. Dinner was new potatoes from the plot with butter and salt. Nothing better.

I keep thinking about my twenties and how sure I was that I'd have it all worked out by forty. Well, I'm forty now. I've had three careers, one marriage, two cities, a lot of therapy and a dog. I'm not where I planned to be. I don't own a house. I don't run a company. But I wake up most days and like the person I am, which younger me would have found impossible to believe. She hated herself quite a lot. Somewhere along the way, through the divorce and the redundancy and the long slow work of being honest with people, I became someone gentler. I'm writing this down because my birthday dinner is tomorrow and everyone will ask what I'm proud of, and I want an answer that isn't a job title. Maybe this is it.

Tomorrow is the day. After two years of training, endless blisters, the stress fracture, the month of physio and all those dark mornings, I'm running the London marathon. My kit is laid out on the bed like a crime scene: shorts, vest with my name on, gels, plasters, the lucky socks Ayo gave me. I've checked the route map four times and the weather forecast eleven times. My parents are driving down at dawn to stand at mile eighteen with a sign. I keep picturing turning onto the Mall and seeing the finish line, and every time I do my stomach flips with nerves and excitement in equal parts. I know it's going to hurt. I know I might have to walk. I don't care. I've been waiting for this for so long. I'll never sleep tonight.

I don't know how to describe this week except that I have been carrying too many things for too many people and something has to give. Dad's care package collapsed on Monday when the agency lost two carers, so I've been driving over every morning before work and every evening after. Work has a major release on Friday and my team is two people down. Ellie has exams and needs help with revision, and Sam's football has been moved to the other side of town. The house is chaos, the fridge is empty, the cat has been sick twice. I made a list tonight and it has forty-two items on it. I read it through and then just put my head down on the kitchen table for a while. I don't even know which thing to start with. All of it, apparently.

Living alone was supposed to feel like freedom, and in the daytime it mostly does. I like choosing what to eat and when to sleep and leaving my books in piles. But the evenings are long now that the clocks have gone back. I come home at six to a dark flat, put the lamps on, make dinner for one and eat it in front of a screen. Sometimes I realise I haven't said a single word out loud since leaving work. I've started talking to the plants, which is either charming or a warning sign. Laura and the others from university all live in other cities now, with partners and babies and lives that fill up their weekends. We message, but it's not the same as having someone drop round. I don't need a crowd. I'd just like one person nearby.

I wanted to record this before it fades. This evening, completely out of the blue, my old teacher Mr. Hassan emailed me. He'd seen the article about the charity in the local paper and wanted to say that he'd always known I'd do something like this. He remembered things I'd forgotten, like the time I organised a bake sale for the flood appeal when I was twelve, and how I used to argue with him about everything in class. He said I was 'difficult in the best way'. I sat at the kitchen table and cried, because when I was at that school I felt like nobody noticed me at all. It turns out someone did. I wrote back for an hour. I'm going to visit him when I'm next home. I'm so grateful he took the time.

Something shifted this week and I want to notice it. For months the grief over Mum has been like weather I couldn't predict, rolling in at the supermarket or in the car or halfway through a meeting. This week it came more gently. I made her lemon cake on Sunday and instead of crying into the bowl I found myself smiling at the memory of her licking the spoon and pretending she hadn't. On Wednesday a song of hers came on the radio and I sang along. I still miss her every day. But I can feel the edges softening, and I can picture a future where she's a warm presence in the background of my life rather than an open wound. Rhiannon, my counsellor, said this might happen. I didn't believe her. I'm starting to now.

I am still furious about what happened at the parents' meeting tonight. The head announced, as if it were good news, that the school is cutting the special needs support assistants from six to two because of the budget. Two. For four hundred children. When I put my hand up and asked how my daughter, who has one-to-one support in her statement, will get the help she is legally entitled to, he said they would 'explore creative solutions'. Several parents clapped him. Clapped. I walked out because I could feel myself about to say something unforgivable. I've drafted an email to the governors, a letter to the local councillor, and a post for the parents' group. I'll send them in the morning when I've calmed down enough to spell properly. My daughter deserves better than creative solutions.

Honestly, I am just bone tired in a way I don't think sleep is going to fix. It isn't one big thing. It's the accumulation: the long commute, the open-plan office where I can't hear myself think, the constant stream of messages that all need answering now, the evening chores, the weekends that fill up with errands and family obligations. I keep waiting for a quiet patch and it never comes. I fell asleep on the sofa at eight tonight and woke at eleven with a crick in my neck and the television talking to itself. I've been drinking more coffee than water. My eyes feel gritty. I'm not sad exactly, I'm just running on empty and I don't know where the next tank of fuel is supposed to come from. Bed now. Alarm at six.

I finally finished the novel. Nine years, four complete rewrites, two agents who said no, one long period where I didn't open the file at all, and a lot of very early mornings at the kitchen table before work. Tonight at eleven I typed the last sentence, sat back, and read it aloud to the empty room. Then I printed the whole thing, all three hundred and twelve pages, just so I could hold it. It's sitting on the table next to me now in a slightly crooked pile. I don't know if anyone will ever publish it. I don't even know if it's good. But it exists, and it exists because I kept going when every sensible part of me wanted to stop. I'm prouder of this than of anything else I've ever done. I'm going to open a bottle of something.

I keep circling around the decision about whether to move back to Lagos. On paper it makes sense. Mum is getting older, my brother is overwhelmed with looking after her, and the company would let me work remotely from there. In practice it means leaving the life I've built here over twelve years: my friends, my flat, the running club, the little routines that make a place feel like yours. I love it here. I'm also aware that I've started to feel like a visitor in my own family, catching up on news through photos and voice notes. Tonight I made a list of everything I'd gain and everything I'd lose and they came out almost equal, which is no help at all. I think the answer will have to come from somewhere other than a list. I'm going to sleep on it again.

The panic started on the train this morning, just outside the tunnel, and for a few minutes I genuinely thought I was dying. My chest went tight, my hands went numb and the carriage seemed to tilt. I got off at the next station and sat on a bench with my head between my knees while a kind woman asked if I was alright and stayed with me until it passed. It's the third one this month. Each time I tell myself it's just anxiety, it can't hurt me, and each time while it's happening I don't believe that at all. Now I'm dreading tomorrow's commute. I'm already planning which carriage to sit in, near the door, near the emergency handle. I've finally made an appointment with the GP. I need this to stop. I'm frightened of my own body.

The festival was everything I hoped for. Three days in a field with Kemi, Jo and Tunde, sleeping in a tent that leaked, eating noodles out of cups, and dancing until the sun came up on Saturday to a band none of us had heard of on Friday. We got sunburnt and then rained on and then sunburnt again. Jo lost her boots in the mud and walked around in plastic bags for a day. On the last night we lay on the grass on the hill above the main stage, watched the lights and the fireworks and talked about everything, school, exes, what we're scared of, what we want. Driving home I was so tired I could barely keep my eyes open, and so happy I kept laughing at nothing. These are my people. I'm keeping this weekend forever.

I cleared my calendar for the whole of today and didn't tell anyone, which I've never done before. I turned my phone off at nine and left it in a drawer. I walked to the bakery for a cinnamon bun, then sat in the window of the café with a notebook and wrote whatever came into my head for an hour. In the afternoon I took the bus to the botanical gardens and wandered the glasshouses, reading the little signs about each plant. I sat by the pond for a long time watching the koi. Nobody needed anything from me. No decisions, no problems, no messages. Coming home I felt lighter and slower, like the whole of me had been put back in the right order. I didn't realise how loud my life had become until I turned it off for a day.

I've been the person in my family who sorts things out for so long that I'd forgotten I was allowed to need anything. Tonight that changed a little. I was on the phone to my brother Femi, ostensibly about Dad's birthday plans, and I just started crying for no clear reason. Instead of panicking or changing the subject, he listened. He asked what was going on, properly, and I told him about the job, the money worries, how lonely I've been since the divorce. He didn't try to fix anything. He just said he was sorry he hadn't noticed and that he'd come and stay next weekend. I sat on the stairs for a long time after we hung up. I didn't know how much I'd needed someone to look after me for once. I'm grateful beyond words.

Lockdown memories came back today out of nowhere. I was clearing out a drawer and found the little notebook where I used to tick off the days we didn't leave the flat. Ninety-three ticks. I remember how quiet the street was, the clapping on Thursdays, the way Aiden and I learned to make bread badly and argued about who used the last of the flour. I remember being frightened for Mum in the care home and not being able to visit, talking to her through a window. It feels like another life. Sitting on the floor with that notebook I felt a strange mix of things, sadness for that version of us, relief it's over, and something like tenderness for how hard we all tried to keep going. I put the notebook back in the drawer. I'm not ready to throw it away.

This is the longest I've been on a waiting list for anything and the frustration is starting to eat at me. Eighteen months ago my GP referred me to the rheumatology clinic because of the joint pain. Since then I have had one letter confirming the referral, one letter saying the waiting time is 'currently longer than usual', and three phone calls where I was told I'm 'in the system'. Meanwhile my hands hurt every morning, I've stopped playing the piano, and I've had to ask Ravi to open jars for me like I'm ninety. I'm forty-four. I've tried going private but it's two hundred pounds just for a first appointment. Every time I ring, the receptionist is perfectly nice and completely unable to help. I'm not angry with her. I'm angry with all of it.

Eleven days until the move to Edinburgh and I'm buzzing in a way I haven't been in years. I've started packing the books, which in my case means packing about thirty boxes and arguing with myself about every single novel. I've found a café near the new flat that does the kind of strong coffee I like. I've joined the climbing gym online already and signed up for a beginner's Gaelic class just because I can. Rana is driving up with me and we've planned a stop in York for the night. I know there'll be hard days, a new job, no friends at first, the dark winters everyone warns me about. But right now all I can feel is that something new is about to begin, and I've been ready for something new for a very long time. Counting down.

I sat down tonight to make a plan for the year, which I've been putting off since January. Instead of the usual list of goals I tried something Dr. Ortiz suggested: writing about what a good ordinary week would look like, not a perfect one. It turned out to be quite simple. Three runs. One dinner with friends. One evening completely on my own with a book. Calling Gran on Sundays. Work that I'm not ashamed of and home by seven most days. Enough sleep. Looking at it written down, almost none of it needs money or luck. It just needs me to say no to more things and protect the time. I feel quietly hopeful that this year could be the one where I stop chasing everything and start living in a way that actually suits me. It's a start.

The house has been quiet since the kids went back to university and I keep finding things that make me stop. Jas's hoodie on the back of the kitchen chair. A note from Kiran on the fridge saying 'buy more cereal pls'. The extra mugs in the dishwasher that I no longer need to use. I'm proud of them, I'm glad they're out there living, and the house is very empty. Dinner for two feels strange after twenty years of cooking for four. Raj and I sat at the table tonight and didn't quite know what to talk about without the kids' chaos to fill the gaps. We laughed about it eventually. I think we'll find our way back to being just us. But tonight the quiet is loud, and I miss the noise more than I expected.

I finished my first year of sobriety today, and I want to write down something other than the number. A year ago I couldn't get through an evening without a bottle and I'd stopped answering the door. I'd missed my niece's christening and lied about why. I'd lost the job, and nearly lost Hana. This year I've been to three hundred and twelve meetings, learned to cook, started running, apologised to the people I hurt, and watched my sponsor, Pete, get his ten-year chip. Hana and I are rebuilding, slowly, carefully. I still want a drink most evenings around six. I just don't have one. Tonight we're having dinner at the little Italian place where we had our first date. I'm proud of myself in a way that I don't need anyone else to approve of.

Long, steady shift on the ward and for once nothing went wrong. Nine patients, all stable, the observations done on time, the drugs round finished before handover. One of the older ladies, Mrs. Tembo, told me about dancing at the Palais in the fifties while I changed her dressing, and I laughed so much the student nurse came to see what was going on. I had a proper lunch break and actually ate my sandwich sitting down. The evening team arrived on time and the handover took ten minutes instead of forty. I drove home with the radio on, made pasta, and now I'm in bed with a book I'll probably fall asleep on. Nothing remarkable, but it's the first shift in weeks that felt like the job I signed up for. More of those, please.

Moved the furniture around in the living room today, which took most of the afternoon. The sofa now faces the window instead of the television, the bookshelves are on the long wall and the desk is in the corner where the light is better in the mornings. I hung the two prints that have been sitting in the hallway since we moved in and finally put up the shelf for the plants. Vacuumed under everything, found a remote control and three pens. Took the old rug to the charity shop and bought a smaller one at the market for twelve pounds. Cooked dal and rice for dinner and froze half. Called the plumber about the dripping tap; he's coming Wednesday morning. Sorted the recycling. Early night planned. That's the whole day, written down so I remember when things were done.

I think I've been angry at my father for most of my life and only today did I let myself feel how much. He rang for my birthday, which he does every year, and spent twenty minutes talking about his golf and his new car and his opinions about my brother's wife. He didn't ask about the baby, or my job, or how I'm coping after the operation. When I tried to tell him I'd been unwell he said 'well, you sound fine' and moved on. After I hung up I stood in the kitchen and shook. I'm forty-two and I'm still waiting for him to see me. I'm starting to understand he probably never will, and I'm furious about the years I spent trying. I don't know what to do with this anger. I just know it's real.

It's been a hard couple of weeks so I want to note that today was genuinely good, in a small, steady way. I woke up before the alarm and felt rested. I went to the market and bought flowers for no reason. I had a long phone call with Chioma in which we laughed about our disastrous school trip to France twenty years ago until we both had tears running down our faces. In the afternoon I finally fixed the wobbly table that has annoyed me for a year. I made a curry from scratch and it was actually nice. I watched the sun go down from the balcony with a cup of tea. None of these things are big. All together they made a day that felt like mine again. I'm glad. I needed one.
